sections.title: Sample spaces and events
sections.summary: The sample space Ω, events as subsets, and operations on events.
sections.text:
The sample space Ω is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. An event is a subset of Ω.
Example: rolling a fair die — Ω = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. The event "an even number" is A = {2,4,6}.
Operations on events: union A∪B (at least one happened), intersection A∩B (both happened), complement A^c (A did not happen).
Disjoint events: A∩B = ∅.

sections.title: The axioms of probability
sections.summary: Kolmogorov's three axioms and the properties that follow from them.
sections.text:
A probability function P satisfies Kolmogorov's axioms:
1. P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
2. P(Ω) = 1.
3. If A1, A2, ... are pairwise disjoint then P(∪Ai) = ΣP(Ai).
Properties: P(A^c) = 1 − P(A); P(∅) = 0; if A⊆B then P(A) ≤ P(B); inclusion–exclusion: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B).
In a symmetric space (all outcomes equally likely): P(A) = |A| / |Ω|.

sections.title: Conditional probability
sections.summary: P(A|B) as restricting the sample space to B, and the multiplication rule.
sections.text:
Conditional probability: given that B happened and P(B) > 0,
P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B).
Intuition: restrict the sample space to B and ask what part of it is also in A.
Multiplication rule: P(A∩B) = P(A|B)·P(B).
Example: roll two dice. Given that the sum is 8, what is the probability that the first die shows 3? There are 5 outcomes with sum 8, and only (3,5) fits, so 1/5.
Speaker notes: a common mistake is to confuse P(A|B) with P(B|A).

sections.title: The law of total probability
sections.summary: Computing P(A) through a partition of Ω into disjoint events.
sections.text:
The law of total probability: if B1,...,Bn partition Ω (disjoint, and their union is Ω) then
P(A) = Σ P(A|Bi)·P(Bi).
Example: 60% of the lab's computers come from maker X and 40% from maker Y. Failure rates: 2% for X, 5% for Y. The probability that a random computer fails: 0.6·0.02 + 0.4·0.05 = 0.032.

sections.title: Bayes' theorem
sections.summary: Reversing a condition: computing P(B|A) from P(A|B), with a medical-test example.
sections.text:
Bayes' theorem: P(B|A) = P(A|B)·P(B) / P(A), where P(A) usually comes from the law of total probability.
Example (medical test): the disease affects 1% of people. The test's sensitivity is 99% (P(+|sick)=0.99), and its false-positive rate is 5% (P(+|healthy)=0.05).
P(sick|+) = 0.99·0.01 / (0.99·0.01 + 0.05·0.99) ≈ 0.167.
Takeaway: even an "accurate" test gives a low probability when the disease is rare — the base rate fallacy.

sections.title: Independence
sections.summary: Independent events, and mutual versus pairwise independence.
sections.text:
A and B are independent if P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B). Equivalently (when P(B)>0): P(A|B) = P(A).
Independence ≠ disjointness! Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent.
Mutual independence of three events also requires P(A∩B∩C) = P(A)P(B)P(C) — pairwise independence is not enough.

sections.title: Discrete random variables
sections.summary: A random variable as a function from Ω to the reals; the probability mass function.
sections.text:
A random variable X is a function X: Ω → ℝ. Its probability mass function is p_X(x) = P(X = x), and Σ p_X(x) = 1.
Example: X = the number of heads in three coin tosses. X ~ Bin(3, 1/2): P(X=k) = C(3,k)·(1/2)^3.

sections.title: Expectation and linearity
sections.summary: The expectation, and linearity of expectation even without independence.
sections.text:
Expectation: E[X] = Σ x·P(X = x).
Linearity of expectation: E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] — always true, even when the variables are dependent!
Example: the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of n elements is 1 (a sum of indicators, each with expectation 1/n).
Variance: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².

concepts.name: Sample space
concepts.definition: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment; an event is a subset of it.

concepts.name: Probability axioms
concepts.definition: Kolmogorov's three axioms: non-negativity, P(Ω)=1, and countable additivity.

concepts.name: Conditional probability
concepts.definition: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B): the probability of A given that B happened.

concepts.name: Law of total probability
concepts.definition: P(A)=ΣP(A|Bi)P(Bi) for a partition B1..Bn of the sample space.

concepts.name: Bayes' theorem
concepts.definition: P(B|A)=P(A|B)P(B)/P(A) — reversing the direction of the condition.

concepts.name: Independence
concepts.definition: A and B are independent if P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).

concepts.name: Random variable
concepts.definition: A function from the sample space to the reals, with a probability mass function.

concepts.name: Expectation
concepts.definition: E[X]=Σx·P(X=x); always linear, even for dependent variables.
